title: Show a webcam its checkerboard in the views a calibration needs, then put the board back in its rack
instruction: Show the camera on the post the calibration board in all the views a calibration needs, then put the board back in its rack.
context: Every robot camera is calibrated, and again whenever it is moved or replaced, by showing it a printed checkerboard in a series of views. A person does it robot by robot, so this upkeep grows with every robot added to the fleets that gather data for AI and put it to work. The ROS camera_calibration tutorial asks for the checkerboard "on the camera's left, right, top and bottom of field of view", "filling the whole field of view" and "tilted to the left, right, top and bottom", and to "hold the checkerboard still" at each step; OpenCV's detector needs every inner corner and white space round the squares. So the 30 x 16 cm board can only be held by its plain grey ends: held by one end it twists down in the grip, and held at the middle of its top edge the fingers cover the white border, so both grippers hold it, one at each top corner.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases: x forward (away from the arms), y to the robot's left; heights above the table. (1) Webcam, fixed: a USB webcam (9 x 3 x 3 cm; 1280 x 720 pixels, focal length 1,100 pixels, 60 degrees across, principal point at the image centre) on a 1.5 cm square post at x 58.5, its lens at x 55.5, y 0, 27 cm up, looking back at the arms 30 degrees down. (2) Rack, fixed: a wooden stand, base x 13.5 to 31, y -13 to 13, 0.8 cm thick, with a 1 cm lip at its front and a sloped rest 18 cm wide under the board. (3) Calibration board, loose: 30 x 16 cm, 3 mm aluminium composite, 0.18 kg. Printed on its front: a checkerboard of 9 x 6 squares of 2 cm (8 x 5 = 40 inner corners) inside a white border 2 cm wide, and a plain grey band 4 cm wide at each end. It leans back 60 degrees from upright in the rack, printed face up toward the webcam, its bottom edge at x 29 against the lip. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: The board's pose is read from the simulation, and each arm's links and fingers from its joints. What the webcam sees is computed from the board's pose and its stated intrinsics (a pinhole camera). A view counts when all 9 x 6 squares are 8 pixels or more inside the image, the board faces the webcam (within 50 degrees), no part of either arm is in front of the squares or their white border as seen from the webcam, the squares span 30 % or more of the image width, the board is 5 mm or more from its rack and 2 cm or more above the table, its corners have moved less than 1 mm in the last 0.5 s, and OpenCV's findChessboardCorners finds all 40 inner corners in the board's image. Nine targets, one view may meet several: near the image's left, right, top and bottom (the ROS calibrator's X or Y measure 0.25 or less / 0.75 or more), close (ROS size measure 0.5 or more: the corner grid covers a quarter of the image), and turned 20 degrees or more with its left, right, top or bottom edge farther from the webcam. Score: 0.08 per target met (0.72 for all nine); 0.8 once all nine are met and OpenCV's calibrateCamera, run on the corners found in the views that met them, gives the focal length within 2 %; 1.0: that, with the board back in its rack (its middle within 1.5 cm and its tilt within 10 degrees of the start), both grippers 5 cm or more from it, still for 1 s. 0 for the rest of the run once the board touches the table outside its rack, falls off the table, or touches the webcam or its post. Doing nothing scores 0. With real parts the webcam records the trial, and OpenCV's findChessboardCorners and calibrateCamera are run on its frames.
reset_notes: Lean the board back in its rack, printed face up, its bottom edge against the lip, as in the screenshot. Nothing is consumed. Simulation: each trial starts the simulator afresh (each inspect-robots run does).
fidelity: Rigid bodies (PhysX), 20 Hz; the board, stand and webcam are at true size. The webcam is not rendered: its view of the board is drawn from the board's pose with the stated intrinsics (an ideal pinhole, no lens distortion, no lighting or blur) for OpenCV's detector, and the arms are boxes round their links and fingers for the line-of-sight test. The printing is visual only.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (both arms drew back; the right gripper went to the board's right grey end again and again but never took it, and the board never left its rack); demo: 1.0
